$comment: The repositories `lypning collect` imports published programs from. Data, not code: adding a source is a one-line diff a reviewer can read, and it ships in the wheel so a pip user gets the same list a checkout has.

A source is a name, a location and a note. The location is either a git URL — shallow-cloned into ~/.lypning/sources, never into the package tree — or a path on this machine, which is read where it lies and never copied.

DISCOVERY IS BY SHAPE, NOT BY NAME. Nothing here says where in a repository the programs are. The importer walks the tree for .jsonl files, samples the first few lines of each, and keeps the ones whose lines parse as JSON objects carrying a non-empty "program" string. That is the whole reason a source may publish under any directory name it likes: matching on a directory name would mean every repository had to be told what to call its evidence, and the first one that disagreed would be invisible.

An import adds to the corpus and NEVER to tests/corpus/sightings. Those files are one-writer-per-session evidence of what ran in THIS repository; someone else's programs written into them would make provenance a lie, and provenance is what the frequency table that ranks work is built on.

$LYPNING_SOURCES adds locations without editing this file — os.pathsep-separated, same two forms, useful for a checkout sitting next to this one. `lypning collect --from LOCATION` overrides the registry entirely for one run.

Nothing from a fetched tree is ever executed, and git hooks in it are disabled on every command that touches it. An imported program is corpus data — text to run the engines against — not a script to run.
